content: Chronotype refers to an individual's natural inclination regarding the times of day they prefer to be active and alert. This attribute determines whether a person is more alert and productive in the early hours of the day (morningness or larks) or during the evening (eveningness or owls). Morning types tend to wake up early and are most alert in the first part of the day, while evening types are more alert in the evening and prefer to go to bed later. Chronotype is also referred to as circadian type, diurnal preference, or diurnal variation. Humans, as diurnal animals, are naturally active during the daytime. Like most diurnal species, human activity-rest patterns are regulated by endogenous circadian rhythms. Normal variations in chronotypes typically involve sleep-wake cycles that deviate by about two hours earlier or later than the average. However, extreme deviations from this range can interfere with an individual's ability to participate in regular work, school, or social activities. When a person's strong lark or owl tendencies prevent them from functioning within societal norms, they may be diagnosed with a circadian rhythm sleep disorder. History The 20th century saw a significant increase in research on sleep and biological rhythms. Notable advancements were made in understanding the molecular, neural, and medical aspects of biological rhythmicity. Nathaniel Kleitman, a physiology professor, published the book Sleep and Wakefulness in 1939 (revised in 1963), which summarized existing knowledge on sleep and introduced the concept of a basic rest-activity cycle. Kleitman, along with his students, including William C. Dement and Eugene Aserinsky, continued research on sleep throughout the 1900s. Modern research into chronotypes began with O. Öquist's 1970 thesis at the University of Göteborg, Sweden, titled Charting Individual Circadian Rhythms. Öquist's work was later refined by O. Östberg, who, in collaboration with J.A. Horne, developed the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) in 1976. The MEQ remains a widely used tool in chronotype research. A shorter version of the MEQ is available online, and researchers worldwide have validated the MEQ for use in various cultural contexts. In 2004, Jacques Taillard and colleagues revised the MEQ scoring system and conducted a component analysis, focusing on middle-aged employed individuals, as the original MEQ had primarily been validated for university-aged subjects. Several other assessment tools have been developed to measure chronotype, including the Circadian Type Inventory (Folkard, 1987), the Composite Morningness Questionnaire (Smith, 1989), the Lark-Owl Chronotype Indicator (LOCI; Roberts, 1999), and the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ; Roenneberg, 2003). Some of these tools are tailored for specific contexts, such as shift work scheduling, travel fatigue, jet lag, athletic performance, or optimizing the timing of medical procedures. Characteristics Most individuals fall somewhere between the extremes of morningness and eveningness, with estimates suggesting that up to half of the population identifies as either morning or evening types. People with similar chronotypes exhibit comparable patterns in activities such as sleep, appetite, exercise, and study. Chronobiology researchers aim to identify objective markers to measure the chronotype spectrum. Horne and Östberg (1976) found that morning types exhibit higher daytime body temperatures with an earlier peak compared to evening types. Morning types also tend to go to bed and wake up earlier, although no differences in total sleep duration were observed. They emphasized the importance of considering age in chronotype assessments, noting that a bedtime of 11:30 PM might indicate a morning type in a student population but an evening type in individuals aged 40–60 years. Clodoré et al. (1986) observed differences in alertness between morning and evening types following a two-hour sleep reduction. Gibertini et al. (1999) measured blood melatonin levels and found that the timing of the melatonin peak (acrophase) was strongly associated with circadian type, while the amplitude of melatonin rhythms was not. Morning types showed a more rapid decline in melatonin levels after the peak compared to evening types. Duffy et al. (1999) reported that while evening types woke later in terms of clock time, morning types woke at a later circadian phase. This means the interval between circadian phase and usual wake time was longer in morning types. Baehr et al. (2000) found that the daily body temperature minimum occurred around 4 AM for morning types and 6 AM for evening types in young adults. This minimum typically occurred in the middle of the eight-hour sleep period but was closer to wake time in evening types. Evening types also exhibited lower nocturnal body temperatures. The temperature minimum occurred about 30 minutes earlier in women than in men. Similar findings were reported by Mongrain et al. (2004). Zavada et al. (2005) suggested that the timing of mid-sleep on free (non-work) days is the best marker for sleep-based chronotype assessments. This measure correlates well with physiological markers such as Dim-Light Melatonin Onset (DLMO) and the daily cortisol rhythm minimum. They also noted that each chronotype category contains a similar proportion of short and long sleepers. Giampietro and Cavallera (2006) reviewed studies examining the relationship between chronotypes, personality traits, and creative thinking. Notes The Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) and other tools have been adapted and validated for various populations and cultural contexts. Chronotype research has implications for understanding individual differences in sleep-wake patterns, optimizing performance, and managing circadian rhythm disorders.
